b: In this month’s pod, John Doran and Luke Turner listen to a pioneering record in which Scott Walker bade farewell to his brothers in song

Make it easy on yourself: brew a fine mahogany-toned cup of tea, fetch a virgin packet of garibaldis from the pantry, nudge the thermostat up another degree centigrade and recline on the cushion-festooned couch… you will have no regrets!

This month on The Quietus Low Culture Podcast, John and Luke turn their attention to one of their all-time totemic cultural artefacts – something which has been hiding in plain sight all along – the highly unusual 1978 farewell album from the Walker Brothers, Nite Flights. Luke remembers first getting to grips with this inimitable LP in a wood cabin in the frigid Nordic wilds while John sees it as more of a culmination of a lifelong interest in the group inculcated originally by his Mum in Liverpool in the 1970s.

The pair look beyond the oversimplified narrative projected onto Scott Walker, one of the most unique pop stars of the last three quarters of a century, and find a thread of chilly modernism, crystalline anxiety and velveteen alienation running through his entire career; and they take the time to praise the work of Gary Leeds and John Maus. From the influence of Bowie and Joni to the mystery of the music flung into The Thames, from the creative use of sandbags to the dream of a burning piano in Haywards Heath, from tears on the chicken in a basket circuit to the merciless, vice-like grip of Newcastle Brown Ale, from Parallels with Joy Division to kinship with Roxy Music, this is a podcast that should resonate with all readers of this site.
